title: CFA Ethics 27: Standard III(A) - who the client is, and whose money soft dollars spend
subtitle: Identifying the party you actually serve, and the limits of commissions traded for research
whyItMatters: The question 'who is the client' sounds obvious until you manage a pension fund: the party paying the fee is the sponsoring company, but the party you owe duties to is the workforce. Answer it wrongly and every decision after it is skewed.
openingQuestion: You manage a company pension fund. The company's board asks you to increase the weighting of the company's own shares. Whom do you owe your duty to?
openingOptions: The company's board, since they signed the contract and pay the fees
The beneficiaries of the pension fund - the employees themselves
Both parties equally, so a compromise has to be found between them
The regulator, since pension funds are subject to special supervision
explanation: With a pension fund, the party that signs and the party that is served are two different people, and Standard III(A) is explicit that the duty runs to the beneficiaries. This is not a technicality: raising the weight of the sponsor's own shares concentrates the pension portfolio's risk in exactly the place the employees' income already depends on - losing the job and the pension at the same moment. The principle extends to every situation with an intermediary: managing an investment fund, the client is the fund and its investors, not whoever introduced you to the mandate.

summary.keyIdea: The party signing the contract and the party being served can be two different people - with a pension fund, the client is the beneficiary and not the company that hired you.
summary.commonMistake: Spending soft dollars on research that serves the firm generally. That is the client's commission money, so it may only be spent for that client's own benefit.

application.title: The question that identifies the client
application.message: Whose money is this, and who bears the consequence if the decision is wrong. The answer names the real client, not the contract.

sections.text: Standard III(A) imposes three duties towards the client: loyalty, prudence, and putting their interest first. The hardest question is usually not what to do, but who the client is here.
When the party signing is not the party served

With a pension fund the company signs the contract, but the employees are the beneficiaries, and the standard is explicit that the duty runs to the beneficiaries. This is not a technicality: raising the weight of the sponsor's own shares concentrates the pension portfolio's risk in exactly the place the employees' income already depends on - losing the job and the pension at once.

sections.label: The principle extends
sections.text: Every situation with an intermediary calls for the same question. Managing an investment fund, the client is the fund under its own governing documents and its investors - not the person who introduced you to the mandate.
Prudence does not mean avoiding risk

A portfolio that is too safe relative to the liabilities it has to meet can itself be imprudent, because it is almost certain to fall short. Prudence means matching the portfolio to the obligation, not minimising volatility.

On soft dollars - the part of trading commissions used to buy research services - the principle is compact: that is the client's money, so what it buys must serve them. Using it to buy your firm's operating systems does not meet that condition.

lines: Ask first: whose money is this.
Every remaining duty flows out of the answer.

diagram.label: The party signing and the party served can differ
The duty runs to the beneficiary
Prudence: decide as a sensible person would with their money
Care: matched to the beneficiary's own objectives

realWorldExample.company: Soft dollars - brokerage commissions traded for research
realWorldExample.description: A portfolio manager pays trading commissions to a broker, and part of that is exchanged for research reports. That commission is the client's money, not the manager's - so Standard III(A) draws a concrete line: research bought with soft dollars must serve the direct interest of the very clients who paid the commission. Buying internal accounting software, or paying the office rent, with soft dollars spends the client's money on your own costs.

quiz.question: With a pension fund, to whom does the Standard III(A) duty run?
options: The company's board, because they pay the management fees
The fund's beneficiaries, not the party that signed the contract
Both parties, with exactly the same degree of priority given
The regulator supervising the operation of the pension fund
quiz.explanation: Here the payer and the party served come apart, and that is precisely the situation Standard III(A) was written to handle. The board commissions the work but does not bear the consequence of it; the regulator sets the rules rather than receiving the duty; and treating both parties as equal claims is simply a way of not answering the question when the two interests pull against each other.

quiz.question: What may soft dollars be spent on?
options: Research serving the direct interest of the clients who paid the commission
General operating overheads of the fund management company itself
Internal accounting software used across the firm's whole operation
Marketing costs incurred in attracting new clients into the fund
quiz.explanation: The line runs through whose money it is and whom it serves: the commission belongs to the client, so what it buys has to come back to them. Overheads, accounting software and marketing all benefit the manager rather than the clients whose trades generated the commission - and the fact that a healthier firm is indirectly good for clients is not close enough to count.

quiz.question: What does the word prudence in Standard III(A) require?
options: Always choose the investment option with the lowest possible risk
Decide as a sensible person would with assets belonging to them
Invest only in assets carrying a high credit rating from an agency
Avoid every investment capable of losing money in the short term
quiz.explanation: Prudence is not the same thing as avoiding risk. A pension portfolio held entirely in deposits can itself be imprudent, because it will not keep pace with inflation and will therefore fall short of the obligation it exists to meet. Ratings and short-term drawdowns are inputs to that judgement, not substitutes for it - the reference point is always the liability being funded.

quiz.question: Why is raising the weight of the sponsor's own shares in a pension fund a problem?
options: Because the rules bar pension funds from holding anyone's shares
Because sponsor shares are always less liquid than the wider market
Because the employees lose their job and their pension at once
Because doing so raises the pension fund's dealing costs overall
quiz.explanation: This is concentration risk in its most dangerous form: the source of income and the retirement savings both depend on a single business, so one failure takes away both at the same moment. There is no blanket prohibition on holding equities, liquidity is not the issue, and dealing costs are trivial beside the risk being described here.

quiz.question: When managing an investment fund, who is the client under Standard III(A)?
options: The parent company that owns the fund management business
The person who introduced you to the fund management role
The investor holding the largest number of fund units
The fund itself and its investors, under the fund's own documents
quiz.explanation: The investment objectives written into the fund's governing documents are what binds you, not the wishes of any one large investor. A parent company owning the manager has its own commercial interest, an introducer has no ongoing claim at all, and a majority unitholder is one client among many - none of them displaces the mandate you were given.

keyTakeaways: The party signing the contract and the party served can be two different people
With a pension fund, the duty runs to the beneficiaries
Prudence is not avoiding risk - an over-safe portfolio can be imprudent too
Soft dollars are the client's money, so what they buy must serve that client
Managing a fund: the client is the fund under its documents, not the introducer

practicePrompt.question: A broker offers to pay for your firm's market data system, in return for you routing more client order flow through them. Assessment?
options: Legitimate, since a market data system supports investment analysis work
Does it serve the clients who paid, and is best execution still achieved
Legitimate if your firm discloses the arrangement in its annual report
An outright breach, since every soft dollar arrangement is prohibited
practicePrompt.explanation: Both questions have to be answerable, and most learners remember only the first. Even where the data system genuinely is research serving clients, pushing order flow to a broker that does not give the best execution price still spends the client's money on your own benefit - just by a different route.
